sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

Copilot's built-in capabilities cover a lot. Copilot can also be extended two ways: MCP servers that connect it to external tools, and Agent Skills — a file-based system for the CLI and cloud agent.

You'll learn:
- The built-in `@` participants that are often overlooked
- Why GitHub Apps-based Copilot Extensions were retired, and how MCP servers replaced them
- Agent Skills — the file-based skill system for CLI and cloud agent
- How to create your own simple skill
- What integrations government and enterprise users should consider

## Built-In Participants You May Have Missed

Beyond `@workspace`, `@terminal`, and `@vscode` (covered in lesson 6-11), Copilot has several other built-in participants.

### `@github` — Deep GitHub Integration

`@github` gives Copilot access to GitHub.com data — repositories, issues, PRs, code search, and release notes — directly in chat. You must be signed into GitHub for this to work.

**Real use cases:**
```
@github What are the latest changes in the React repository's changelog?
@github Search for open-source Python libraries that handle PDF generation
@github What does this repository's README say about installation requirements?
@github Find examples of how developers typically implement OAuth2 PKCE flow in Node.js
```

### Vision for Copilot — Image Input

Copilot supports image input in Chat. You can paste or drag in:
- A screenshot of an error message — ask Copilot to explain and fix
- A UI mockup or wireframe — ask Copilot to generate the HTML/CSS
- A diagram or flowchart — ask Copilot to implement it as code
- A screenshot of legacy software — ask Copilot to recreate it with modern code

To use it: in Copilot Chat, click the paperclip icon and attach an image, or drag an image into the chat input.

## Copilot Extensions Have Been Retired — MCP Is the Replacement

GitHub previously offered Copilot Extensions: GitHub Apps that integrated with Copilot Chat and appeared as `@extension-name` participants once installed from the GitHub Marketplace. **GitHub sunset this entire system on November 10, 2025**, retiring GitHub Apps-based Copilot Extensions in favor of MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers. If you come across older material describing `@docker`, `@azure`, or similar installable Copilot Extensions, that path no longer works — the Marketplace's Copilot Extensions category was removed after the sunset date.

### What Replaced It

The vendors that used to publish Copilot Extensions — Docker, Azure, Atlassian (Jira/Confluence), Datadog, Sentry, and others — now offer the same integrations as MCP servers instead. Instead of installing an app to your GitHub account, you add a server entry to `.vscode/mcp.json` (or your organization's MCP configuration), and the vendor's tools become available to Copilot Agent Mode and Chat. Lesson 6-17 covers MCP setup in depth, including multi-server configurations and government-relevant servers like Azure DevOps.

**One practical difference to know:** the old Extensions were tied to your GitHub account and worked the same way on every surface (VS Code, GitHub.com, mobile). MCP servers are configured per client — a server you add to one machine's `.vscode/mcp.json` isn't automatically available on GitHub.com or a colleague's IDE unless they configure it too (or your organization deploys it centrally).

### How to Find Current Integrations

1. In VS Code, open the Command Palette (`Ctrl+Shift+P`) and run **MCP: Browse Servers** to see the gallery of available MCP servers (or search `@mcp` in the Extensions view).
2. GitHub also maintains an MCP registry that VS Code and other clients can pull server listings from.
3. Check the vendor's own docs (Docker, Datadog, Atlassian, etc.) — most now publish an official MCP server rather than a Copilot Extension.

### Finding Integrations for Government Work

Search the MCP server gallery or your vendor's documentation for:
- ServiceNow, Jira/Confluence integrations
- Microsoft 365 integrations
- Security scanning tools
- Documentation generators

Then follow the MCP setup pattern from lesson 6-17 to connect them.

## Agent Skills — File-Based Extensions for the CLI

Agent Skills are a different kind of extension, designed specifically for the GitHub Copilot CLI and cloud agent. Instead of a GitHub App, a Skill is a folder containing:
- A `SKILL.md` file — describes what the skill does and when to use it
- Optional scripts, templates, or resource files the skill needs

### How Skills Work

When you're in a CLI session or using the cloud agent, Copilot scans available skills and decides which ones are relevant to the current task. When it chooses a skill, the `SKILL.md` is injected into the agent's context — giving it the instructions, scripts, and examples it needs.

You don't invoke skills manually — they load automatically when relevant.

### Installing Skills with `gh skill`

```bash
# Discover available skills
gh skill search [query]

# Install a skill from GitHub
gh skill install [owner/repo]

# List your installed skills
gh skill list

# Update a skill
gh skill update [skill-name]
```

### Writing Your Own Skill

Create a folder for your skill with a `SKILL.md`. A SKILL.md file is Markdown with YAML frontmatter requiring, at minimum, a `name` and a `description` (an optional `license` field is also supported). There is no separate keyword-list field — Copilot decides whether a skill is relevant by matching the current task against your `description`, so the description itself needs to say clearly and specifically when the skill applies.

**Example: A government report generation skill**

Create `~/.copilot/skills/gov-report/SKILL.md`:
```markdown
---
name: gov-report
description: Generates government-format reports from data files. Use whenever the user asks to create, format, summarize, or export an administrative report, or export data as a report.
---

# Government Report Generation Skill

## Standard Report Format

All reports must include:
1. Header: Report title, generation date, department name
2. Executive summary: 3-5 sentences, plain English
3. Data section: tabular format, no more than 10 columns
4. Findings: numbered list of key observations
5. Footer: data source, processing timestamp, operator name

## File Naming Convention

`DEPT_REPORTTYPE_YYYYMMDD_vN.csv` where N increments if the file already exists.

## Required Output Validation

Before finalizing any report:
- Verify no PII columns are included (names, SSNs, addresses)
- Verify all dates are in YYYY-MM-DD format
- Verify total row count matches source file
- Log the run to audit.log with: timestamp, source file, output file, row count
```

When you ask Copilot CLI to "generate a monthly report from transactions.csv", it matches the request against this skill's description, loads it, and applies all the standards automatically.

**Skills vs. Custom Instructions — when to use each:**
- **Custom instructions** (`.github/copilot-instructions.md`): Rules that apply to every single interaction in a repository. Best for: coding standards, naming conventions, error handling patterns.
- **Agent Skills**: Domain-specific expertise that loads on demand, only when the task matches the skill's description. Best for: complex workflows with specific steps, government reporting formats, specialized tooling procedures.

Think of custom instructions as the background rules that are always on, and skills as specialized reference cards that activate when the situation calls for them.

sections.title: Explore the MCP Server Gallery
sections.content:
Find and evaluate MCP servers relevant to your work — the current replacement for the retired Copilot Extensions marketplace.

**Step 1 — Open the MCP server gallery.**
In VS Code, open the Command Palette (`Ctrl+Shift+P`) and run **MCP: Browse Servers** (or search `@mcp` in the Extensions view).

**Step 2 — Browse with intent.** You're looking for servers that connect to tools you actually use. Answer these questions as you browse:
- Do you use any cloud platform (Azure, AWS, GCP)? Is there a server?
- Do you use Jira, Linear, or another project tracker?
- Do you use Datadog, Sentry, or another monitoring tool?
- Do you use Docker or Kubernetes?
- Are there any government-specific tools listed?

**Step 3 — Install one server** that looks useful for your actual work (into your user profile or the current workspace).

**Step 4 — Use it.** Open Copilot Chat in Agent Mode and ask a real question from your work that requires the tool the server provides.

**Step 5 — Evaluate:**
- Did it connect to the right data?
- Was the response accurate and useful?
- Would you use this in your actual workflow?
- What would you use it for specifically?

**Document:** Write one sentence on what this server does well and one sentence on its limitations.

sections.title: Workshop A — Build Your First Agent Skill
sections.content:
Create a custom agent skill for a task you do repeatedly.

**Step 1 — Identify a repeated task.** Think of something you do regularly in the terminal that involves multiple steps, specific formats, or rules you have to remember. Examples:
- Processing a specific type of data file
- Generating a report in a specific format
- Reviewing code for a specific type of issue
- Running a specific deployment checklist

**Step 2 — Create the skill folder:**
```
mkdir -p ~/.copilot/skills/my-skill-name
```

**Step 3 — Write the SKILL.md:**
```markdown
---
name: my-skill-name
description: [A specific sentence or two describing what this skill does and exactly when Copilot should use it — this is what Copilot matches against your request, so be precise]
---

# [Skill Name]

## When to Use This Skill
[Describe the scenarios where this skill applies]

## Steps
1. [Step 1 with specific details]
2. [Step 2]
3. [Step 3]

## Rules
- [Specific rule 1]
- [Specific rule 2]

## Output Format
[Describe what the output should look like]
```

**Step 4 — Test it.** Start a Copilot CLI session and ask it to do the task your skill covers. Watch whether it uses your skill (the SKILL.md content appears in the references).

**Step 5 — Refine.** If the skill wasn't triggered, make the `description` more specific about when it applies. If it was triggered but didn't apply the rules correctly, make the rules more specific.

**Outcome:** A persistent agent skill that improves Copilot's performance on your specific repeated task — every time, automatically.

sections.title: Workshop B — Vision for Copilot: Image to Code
sections.content:
Use Copilot's image input capability to convert visual content into working code.

**Choose one of these real scenarios:**

**Scenario A — UI Screenshot to Code**
Take a screenshot of any form, dashboard, or table from any website or app. In Copilot Chat:
- Paste the image (Ctrl+V or drag into chat)
- Ask: 'Recreate this UI as clean HTML and CSS. Make it responsive.'
- Evaluate: does the output match the screenshot layout?

**Scenario B — Error Screenshot to Fix**
Take a screenshot of any error message — from your terminal, a browser, any application. In Copilot Chat:
- Paste the screenshot
- Ask: 'What does this error mean and how do I fix it? Be specific about the file and line.'
- Evaluate: is the analysis accurate without you typing out the error text?

**Scenario C — Government Form/Document to Data Structure**
Take a screenshot of any form, table, or structured document from your work (remove any real sensitive data). In Copilot Chat:
- Paste the screenshot
- Ask: 'Generate a Python dataclass (or JSON schema) that models this data structure. Include field names, types, and any validation rules visible in the form.'
- Evaluate: does the generated structure match the form's fields?

**Document:** Which scenario worked best? What was the quality of the image-to-code conversion? Where would you use this in real work?

sections.title: Workshop C — Government Workflow Skill Library
sections.content:
Build a library of 3 agent skills tailored for government/administrative work.

**Skill 1 — Data Quality Checker**
Create a skill that activates when you ask to validate or clean a dataset. The skill should specify:
- How to check for duplicate rows
- How to check for required fields
- How to flag out-of-range values
- What to log and report
- The format of the validation report output

**Skill 2 — Compliance Review**
Create a skill that activates when reviewing code or scripts for compliance. The skill should specify:
- What PII patterns to look for
- What audit logging requirements to check
- What access control patterns to verify
- How to format the compliance finding report

**Skill 3 — Report Standardizer**
Create a skill that activates when generating reports. The skill should specify:
- Required header and footer format
- Required columns and their order
- Date format requirements
- Naming conventions
- What to log to the audit trail

**Test all three** in a Copilot CLI session by giving tasks that should trigger each skill.

**Outcome:** A skill library that makes Copilot your specialized government workflow assistant — not a generic coding AI.

sections.question: You want Copilot to connect to your monitoring tool (e.g., Datadog) the way older tutorials describe installing a Copilot Extension like @datadog from the GitHub Marketplace. What should you actually do in 2026?
options: Go to github.com/marketplace and filter by Copilot, exactly as before — nothing has changed
Nothing replaces this — GitHub removed the capability with no alternative

Connect the tool as an MCP server instead — GitHub retired GitHub Apps-based Copilot Extensions on November 10, 2025, and vendors like Datadog now publish MCP servers you configure per client (e.g., in .vscode/mcp.json)
Install it using `gh skill install` — Agent Skills replaced Extensions
sections.explanation: GitHub Apps-based Copilot Extensions (the @extension-name marketplace system) were sunset on November 10, 2025, in favor of MCP servers. Vendors that used to publish Copilot Extensions — Datadog included — now offer the same integration as an MCP server. You add it to your MCP configuration rather than installing a GitHub App, and unlike the old account-wide Extensions, MCP servers are configured per client. Agent Skills are a separate system (Markdown instructions for the CLI/cloud agent) and are not a replacement for tool integrations.

sections.question: What is the main difference between an MCP server and an Agent Skill?
options: MCP servers cost money; Skills are free

MCP servers give Copilot tool calls into external systems (databases, Jira, GitHub, monitoring tools, etc.); Agent Skills are Markdown files with instructions/scripts that load automatically into the CLI/cloud agent when a task matches the skill's description
MCP servers work only in VS Code; Skills work only in the terminal
MCP servers require administrator approval; Skills can be installed by any user
sections.explanation: MCP servers connect Copilot to external systems — a database, Jira, GitHub, a monitoring tool — by exposing tool calls Copilot can invoke (covered in depth in lesson 6-17). Agent Skills are Markdown files (SKILL.md) stored locally or in your repository — they load automatically when the CLI or cloud agent matches the task against the skill's description, without you invoking them explicitly, and they don't call external systems on their own. MCP servers are for integrating external tools and data; Skills are for codifying your own expertise and procedures.

sections.content: **Lesson 6-16 complete.** Copilot's extension ecosystem — MCP servers for external tools (which replaced the retired Copilot Extensions marketplace), agent skills for your own procedures, and the built-in @github participant for repository search — significantly expands what Copilot can do. The most powerful combination for professional work: connect MCP servers for your core tools (Azure, Jira, monitoring), and write skills for your team's specific workflows. Lesson 6-17 covers Advanced MCP — connecting multiple external systems simultaneously and chaining their tools together in a single prompt.
